measurement.happened:
This week in Ukraine was defined by a dramatic escalation of the war of bridges, a high-stakes trilateral summit that left Kyiv feeling sidelined, and a sharp spike in Russian missile and drone barrages that killed civilians across the country. I will walk through the main themes one by one.

THE CRIMEAN BRIDGE AND THE WAR OF BRIDGES. The single most consequential military event of the week was Ukraine's repeated strikes on the Kerch Bridge (the Crimean Bridge) linking Russia to occupied Crimea. On November 16, Ukraine launched what the defence ministry called the biggest drone attack of the war, with over 1,300 drones sent toward Russian territory. A section of the bridge was hit and partially collapsed on November 17. Ukraine struck it again on November 18 and 19, using European-made Ruta missiles, which the company said were the only foreign weapons in the operation. Zelensky called it an unprecedented operation and said it was a fair response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Russia's Kremlin aide and Putin himself vowed a far more painful response. Bloomberg reported that cleanup would take Russia months, effectively turning Crimea into a more isolated peninsula. Ukraine also hit two oil refineries in Krasnodar and a facility in Tatarstan, and Russia reported that more of its regions were limiting fuel sales as refinery output dropped. The Financial Times noted that the drone war was even sending optical fibre prices soaring globally. This theme is supported by headlines from Reuters, BBC, CNN, Bloomberg, Financial Times, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, and Deutsche Welle.

THE TRUMP-PUTIN-XI SUMMIT AND EUROPE'S ANXIETY. On November 19, Trump met Putin for the first time in fifteen months, with Xi hosting the trilateral meeting at the APEC summit. Trump called Putin a friend and said he had a great relationship with him. He said he would not make deals with Putin without Ukraine, and that he wanted a peace deal before January. But the optics were painful for Kyiv and its allies. Zelensky, speaking to CNN and in public remarks, said for us he is a killer, a direct rebuke to Trump's friendly language. Ukrainian residents in Kyiv told TV5Monde they felt like three losers watching the meeting. UK's Prince Harry, who had surprised everyone with a visit to Ukraine on November 16 to visit wounded veterans and tell them you are going to win the war, warned of a big separation between the US administration and the US public on support for Ukraine. Ukraine's allies met in Berlin on November 19, a day after the trilateral summit, to present a united front and counter what they called Yalta 2.0 optics. Germany's Chancellor Merz said Europe would join new peace talks soon. France's Macron said Ukraine's NATO membership was relevant for European security. The US floated the idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, which Zelensky confirmed. Russia's deputy foreign minister Ryabkov said Russia rejected any deal letting Ukraine join NATO, and Russia pushed back against the US idea of NATO-style security guarantees, though Kushner said Russia was comfortable with them. This theme is supported by Reuters, AFP, BBC, CNN, Bloomberg, Financial Times, Wall Street Journal, CNBC, Al Jazeera, and TV5Monde.

RUSSIA'S RETALIATORY STRIKES AND CIVILIAN CASUALTIES. In direct response to the bridge strikes, Russia unleashed what Zelensky called one of its largest attacks. On November 20, a rain of missiles and drones hit Kyiv, damaging two bridges and causing water and power cuts. The Dutch and Austrian embassies were damaged. On November 21, a ballistic missile hit Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, killing two and wounding scores, including a seven-year-old and an emergency worker in a double-tap strike. Odesa was hit on November 18, killing four. In total, at least eight were killed in the November 20 barrage, and dozens more were reported dead or missing in the days before US talks. France sought a UN Security Council meeting after the strikes on Kyiv. The EU accused Russia of stalling peace talks to target power plants as winter approached. This theme is supported by Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, Deutsche Welle, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, and Wall Street Journal.

EUROPEAN MILITARY AND FINANCIAL COMMITMENTS. Despite the US-centric diplomacy, Europe moved to deepen its military and financial support for Ukraine. The EU proposed a fresh 45 billion euro loan for Ukraine, to be serviced in part by tapping the profits on Russian frozen assets. The IMF said it was near a 1.6 billion dollar deal with Ukraine. The UK pledged more than 1,000 short-range missiles and long-range drones as part of a 260 million pound package. Germany backed a new Ukrainian drone production venture with Auterion and Skyfall. France is sending soldiers into Ukraine under a mission called Volia. Troops from eleven European countries held a drill in Poland for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine. Britain's Health Secretary Wes Streeting visited Kyiv on November 21 and called Putin a cold-blooded killer. California's Governor Newsom visited and donated 1,300 hospital beds. This theme is supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, Bloomberg, Financial Times, TV5Monde, and Al Jazeera.

THE STARSHIELD DISPUTE. Zelensky publicly clashed with Elon Musk over restrictions on Starshield (SpaceX's satellite internet) in Ukraine. Zelensky said the restrictions were hurting Ukraine's ability to counter jet-powered drones and threatened its energy defenses ahead of winter. Musk accused Zelensky of lying. Trump's intelligence chief reportedly warned that no funding for SpaceX without answers on the Starshield slowdown. Zelensky urged the US and Musk to lift the restrictions and be on the right side of history. This theme is supported by Reuters, BBC, CNN, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle, and TV5Monde.

DENMARK AND THE ASSASSINATION PLOT. Denmark accused Russian intelligence of plotting to assassinate a US-Ukrainian rapper on Danish soil. Two Danes were suspected of being hired by Russia. Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat. This was a notable intelligence incident that added a new layer of tension between Russia and a NATO ally. This theme is supported by Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, Wall Street Journal, Al Jazeera, and TV5Monde.

OTHER NOTABLE ITEMS. An investigation concluded that Russia used tear gas against Ukrainian troops, a potential chemical weapons issue. Ukraine criticized the IAEA for appointing a sanctioned Russian official to a senior nuclear post. A Russian was arrested for spying on Palantir over its Ukraine support. Finland reported a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian cargo in the Baltic Sea. A nuclear safety warning said the risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine was increasing this winter. Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, described as melding man and machine to repel Russian forces, was highlighted. The drone war was also producing a new category of technology: flying modems that helped guide the bridge strikes, and drone-ambulances for the dead zone. The Financial Times noted that Russia was importing record volumes of petrol as Ukraine struck refineries. A Russian filmmaker, after near death, resolved to confront Putin's war. Prince Harry's surprise visit generated significant media attention. The WTA Finals saw Russia's Andreeva defeat Ukraine's Svitolina, a small but symbolically noted sports result.
measurement.expected:
Looking ahead to the week of November 21 through roughly November 28, 2026, here is what I expect, theme by theme, with my confidence level stated in plain words.

RUSSIAN STRIKES ON ENERGY AND INFRASTRUCTURE. Almost certain. Russia has already hit Kyiv's bridges, Odesa, and Zelensky's hometown in the last three days, and the EU has accused Moscow of targeting power plants as winter nears. With the nuclear accident risk warning already issued and the Starshield restrictions still limiting Ukraine's air defense against jet-powered drones, I expect at least one more large-scale Russian missile and drone barrage on energy infrastructure, possibly targeting the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant vicinity or major substations. Zelensky will likely call for emergency energy measures. The winter heating season is ramping up, and every day without power is more costly.

PEACE TALKS FORMAT AND FIRST ROUND. Probable. Merz said Europe would join talks soon. Kushner said Russia is comfortable with NATO-like guarantees. Trump wants a deal before January. I expect that within this week, the format will be nailed down: likely a US-EU-Ukraine-Russia track, possibly in a neutral venue or split between Washington and a European capital. The first substantive round may not happen until the following week, but the scheduling, the list of delegates, and the agenda (territory, security guarantees, NATO membership, sanctions relief) will be announced. There is a real chance the first meeting is set for early December, but the groundwork and preliminary bilateral contacts will happen this week. I am less certain about whether Russia will actually sit at the table with Europe present, since the Kremlin aide denied that Europeans would join the next round. So the format could be a US-Russia bilateral with Ukraine in a separate track, which would anger Kyiv and Brussels.

CRIMEA BRIDGE AFTERMATH AND LOGISTICS. Almost certain. Bloomberg said cleanup takes months. I expect Russia to divert more fuel and military supplies through land routes or the Sea of Azov, increasing vulnerability to further Ukrainian strikes. Ukraine will likely continue hitting Russian refineries and fuel depots to compound the logistics pain. More Russian regions may restrict fuel sales. The symbolic blow to Putin's showpiece will be a recurring talking point in every diplomatic meeting this week.

EUROPEAN COMMITMENTS AND THE LOAN. Probable. The 45 billion euro EU loan proposal is on the table. I expect the European Council or a special meeting to move toward a political agreement on the loan, with the mechanism of using Russian frozen asset profits to service it being debated. The IMF 1.6 billion dollar deal is close to final. I also expect at least one more European country to announce a new military package (missiles, drones, air defense) as a show of solidarity, especially after the Berlin summit and the Poland drill. The Coalition of the Willing will likely issue a joint statement reaffirming support.

STARSHIELD DISPUTE. Possible. The Zelensky-Musk spat is very public and Trump's intelligence chief has inserted himself. I expect either a technical compromise (partial lifting of restrictions in specific combat zones) or a continued stalemate with Zelensky making another public appeal. If the dispute is not resolved before the first peace talks, it will become a bargaining chip. I would not bet on a full resolution this week, but a dialogue or a partial easing is possible.

DENMARK-RUSSIA DIPLOMATIC TENSION. Probable. Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat. I expect Russia to respond with a tit-for-tat expulsion or a sharp note. This will be a smaller but persistent diplomatic irritant. It may also feed into broader NATO discussions about Russian intelligence activity in Europe.

UKRAINE'S DEEP STRIKES. Probable. Having hit the bridge and refineries, Ukraine will likely continue targeting Russian energy and logistics infrastructure, especially if the bridge disruption is confirmed to last months. I expect strikes on additional refineries, rail hubs, or military airfields. The US has urged Kyiv to focus on front-line equipment rather than deep strikes, but Germany and the UK have backed the deep-strike strategy, so I expect Ukraine to continue both.

ZALENSKY DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE NATO REFERENDUM IDEA. Possible. Zelensky said he is ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum. If the US and EU push the NATO-membership-for-Donbas trade this week, Zelensky may announce a timeline for a referendum or a public consultation. This would be a significant domestic political move. I am less certain it happens within seven days, but the groundwork and public messaging will likely begin.

WINTER AND ENERGY CRISIS. Almost certain. The nuclear accident risk warning, the Starshield limits, the Russian strikes on power plants, and the approaching cold all point to a worsening energy situation. I expect blackouts in at least one major city, calls for emergency fuel imports, and possibly a declaration of a state of emergency in the energy sector if a major substation is hit.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES (things I would consider but would not bet heavily on):
- A sudden Russian offer for a short ceasefire during the holiday season (Christmas/New Year) as a goodwill gesture before talks. Possible but not likely this week.
- A second major strike on the Crimean Bridge or a strike on the remaining operational lanes, escalating the bridge war further. Possible if Russia's retaliation cycle continues.
- A dramatic shift in US position, such as Trump announcing a specific peace framework with territorial concessions. Possible given his January deadline, but the details would need to be worked out first.
- A Ukrainian counteroffensive or significant territorial gain on one sector, possibly using the new drone-ambulance and man-machine systems from Operation Vivaldi. Unlikely to be a major shift, but a local success is possible.
- The IAEA nuclear safety issue escalating into a formal dispute if a minor incident occurs at Zaporizhzhia. Unlikely but the risk is elevated.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON THIS WEEK:
- A full ceasefire or formal peace agreement signed. The pieces are not in place. The format is not set, the territory question is unresolved, and both sides are still in escalation mode.
- Ukraine formally ceding Donbas or any territory. The US floated the idea, but Zelensky has not accepted it, and a domestic referendum or parliamentary vote would take time.
- Russia formally accepting NATO membership for Ukraine or a NATO-style security guarantee in writing. Kushner's comfort is not the same as a Kremlin position, and Ryabkov already rejected it.
- A major ground offensive by either side. The war is in a drone-and-missile phase, and neither side appears ready for a large-scale ground push in late November.
- A complete resolution of the Starshield dispute. It is a multi-party issue involving SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the Ukrainian military, and it is unlikely to be fully settled in seven days.
- A new major diplomatic incident like the Denmark assassination plot, though a smaller intelligence-related event is possible.
emoji_reasons: The dominant story of the week was the war of bridges: Ukraine's record drone barrage that partially collapsed the Crimean Bridge, Russia's vow of painful retaliation, and the subsequent missile barrages that killed civilians in Kyiv, Odesa, and Zelensky's hometown, making bombing and airstrikes the defining image of the week.

The Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral summit, the Berlin Coalition of the Willing summit, the EU's 45 billion euro loan proposal, and the push to include Europe in peace talks made international diplomacy and multilateral summits the second most important thread of the week.

Peace negotiations, the US-floated NATO-membership-for-Donbas trade, the scheduling of Europe-Russia-Ukraine talks, and the Kushner-Rubio diplomatic shuttle all centered on negotiations and backchannel talks, making this the third key theme.

delta.motion: The most dramatic growth between the two photographs is in the scale and symbolism of Ukrainian drone warfare. In the first week, Ukraine was hitting refineries and pumping stations, a grinding economic campaign that was reducing Russia's oil processing capacity. By the second week, Ukraine had escalated to striking the Crimean Bridge, the single most visible and politically charged Russian infrastructure asset, using over 1,300 drones in what the defence ministry called the biggest attack of the war, and following up with European-made Ruta missiles. The target shifted from economic pressure to strategic and psychological blow. Russia's import of record petrol volumes and further fuel rationing confirm the economic thread continued, but the bridge became the headline. The second major growth is in European commitment. In the first week, Europe was still fighting over who to send and whether to get a seat at the table. By the second week, the EU had proposed a 45 billion euro loan, the UK pledged over a thousand missiles, France was sending soldiers into Ukraine under a mission called Volia, Germany backed a new drone production venture, and eleven European nations held a joint drill in Poland. The argument became action. The Starshield dispute also grew in intensity and personalness. In week one, Zelensky complained about speed limits and senators ordered records preserved. In week two, Musk accused Zelensky of lying directly, and Trump's intelligence chief threatened to withhold SpaceX funding until answers came. The controversy moved from a technical grievance to a personal and political confrontation. Russian retaliatory strikes grew in severity, from a massive overnight barrage in week one to what Zelensky called one of Russia's largest attacks in week two, including a ballistic missile on his own hometown of Kryvyi Rih and damage to two Kyiv bridges. Several themes shrank or disappeared entirely. India's role as a potential Black Sea mediator, which was a distinct thread in the first week, vanished completely from the second. The car bombings in Moscow, the Chernobyl arch fundraising, the South Africa arrests, and the UForce funding round all dropped out of the news cycle. The prisoner exchange, which was expected to produce visible logistics and a small ceremony, did not surface as a headline in the second week, suggesting either it happened quietly or it is still in bureaucratic limbo. New themes appeared that had no counterpart in the first photograph. The Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral summit at the APEC meeting in China was entirely new and reframed the entire diplomatic picture around the US president rather than his envoys. The Denmark assassination plot, in which Russia allegedly hired two Danes to kill a US-Ukrainian rapper, introduced a new intelligence-warfront layer. Prince Harry's surprise visit to wounded veterans in Kyiv was a new and highly visible public-diplomacy event. The tear gas investigation, the IAEA controversy over a sanctioned Russian official, the nuclear safety warning about rising accident risk this winter, the Palantir spy arrest, and the emergence of flying modems and drone-ambulances as new technology categories all appeared for the first time. The overall motion is one of escalation in both military action and diplomatic stakes, with the centre of gravity shifting from a multi-actor process involving envoys, the EU, and India to a much more concentrated and personal confrontation between Trump, Putin, and Zelensky, with Europe transitioning from a supplicant to a committed military partner.
delta.wind: On the Donbas-for-NATO proposal, the expectation was that it would be the dominant standalone headline. It was confirmed and discussed, and Russia formally rejected any deal letting Ukraine join NATO, but it became a thread within the larger Trump-Putin-Xi summit story rather than the headline in its own right. Zelensky did not schedule a referendum in this window. The expectation was partially right in substance but wrong in framing. On a second round of talks or preparatory meetings, the expectation was that preparatory contacts were almost certain and a formal second round was probable. What actually happened was a trilateral summit at APEC, which is neither a formal second round of the Abu Dhabi process nor a simple preparatory meeting. It is a new format. Europe met in Berlin the next day and Merz said it would join talks soon, so the preparatory phase is ongoing but the formal second round has not yet occurred. The expectation was directionally correct but the form was different. On the prisoner exchange, the expectation was that at least the first batch would move. The second photograph does not mention the exchange at all, so it either happened quietly without headlines or is still stuck in logistics. The expectation was probably right on the substance but the visibility was lower than forecast. On Russian strikes on energy and winter blackouts, the expectation was almost certain and it was strongly confirmed. Russia launched what Zelensky called one of its largest attacks, hit two Kyiv bridges, caused water and power cuts, and fired a ballistic missile at Kryvyi Rih. The EU explicitly accused Russia of stalling talks to hit power plants as winter approached. This was the most accurately forecast theme. On Ukraine's drone strikes on Russian oil, the expectation was continued and expanded attacks on refineries with a possible new high-profile strike. The refineries in Krasnodar and Tatarstan were hit, and Russia's petrol imports hit record levels, confirming the economic thread. But the high-profile strike of the week was the Crimean Bridge, which was not in the expectation at all. The expectation captured the oil campaign but missed the strategic leap to the bridge. On the Starshield controversy, the expectation was that it would intensify or generate more headlines, possibly with a US political firestorm. It intensified in a more personal and confrontational form than forecast: Musk accused Zelensky of lying, and Trump's intelligence chief threatened funding. The expectation was right on the direction and roughly right on the intensity, though the personal clash between Musk and Zelensky was sharper than the technical dispute that was anticipated. On the EU budget and funding fight, the expectation was more public sparring and a draft funding package. What happened was more positive: the EU proposed a 45 billion euro loan, the UK pledged missiles, and France sent troops. The sparring was less visible than expected and the concrete commitments were larger. The expectation underestimated Europe's willingness to commit. On Baltic and maritime tension, the expectation was at least one more incident. Finland reported a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian cargo vessel in the Baltic Sea, confirming the forecast. On Russian domestic pressure, the expectation was visible frustration, small protests, or a security crackdown. The petrol rationing and record imports confirm the economic strain, but no major protests or visible crackdown appeared in the headlines. The expectation was probably too optimistic about how quickly domestic pressure would become visible. On India's Black Sea corridor push, the expectation was a concrete proposal or joint statement. India does not appear in the second photograph at all. This expectation did not come true in the observed window. Among the less-likely surprises, Zelensky did not call a snap referendum, a direct Zelensky-Putin meeting did not happen (they were in the same room at APEC but Trump was between them), Russia did not formally accept the five-nation European team yet, and no new EU sanctions package was formally adopted. All of these were correctly judged as unlikely in this window. Among the things not bet on, no full ceasefire, no Zelensky resignation, no full-scale new offensive, no Chernobyl nuclear incident, no formal NATO membership, and no warship sinking all held true as expected. What was not expected and did appear: the Crimean Bridge as the dominant military event, the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral format, the Denmark assassination plot, Prince Harry's visit, the tear gas investigation, the IAEA controversy, France sending troops into Ukraine, the nuclear safety warning, the Palantir spy arrest, and the new technology categories of flying modems and drone-ambulances. The pattern of error is consistent: the expectation correctly tracked the known threads (oil strikes, Starlink, EU funding, Russian energy strikes) but underweighted the probability of a single dramatic, symbolic military event (the bridge) that would reframe the entire week. It also underweighted the personal diplomacy of the US president stepping in directly, and it overestimated the visibility of smaller threads (India, prisoner exchange logistics) that either resolved quietly or fell out of the news cycle. The expectation treated the week as a continuation of the previous week's trajectory, but the actual week was defined by a step-change in both military and diplomatic escalation that no single thread from the first photograph predicted.
delta.driver: The force pushing Ukraine from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a military escalation that Ukraine chose to make before diplomacy could lock in terms, and a diplomatic track that the United States is trying to close before the January deadline. Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge not merely as a military target but as a bargaining chip, a way to say that the cost of Russian occupation is not just refineries and pipelines but the physical lifeline to Crimea itself, and to force any peace negotiation to account for that cost. At the same time, Trump, who had been working through envoys, stepped onto the stage personally at APEC, meeting Putin face-to-face with Xi as host, and the optics of that meeting, with Zelensky calling Trump's friend a killer and Ukrainian residents feeling like three losers, created a pressure for Europe to assert itself and for Ukraine to keep demonstrating that it is not a passive party in its own peace deal. Winter is the hard deadline that compresses all of this: Russia's strikes on power and water infrastructure become existential as temperatures drop, Ukraine's grid is already under stress, and the EU's 45 billion euro loan and the IMF's near-finalised deal are attempts to keep the economy and the military going through the coldest months. The fundamental driver is a race between military leverage and diplomatic closure, with the Crimean Bridge as the physical symbol of that race, and with every actor, Kyiv, Moscow, Washington, Brussels, and now Beijing, trying to set the terms before the window shuts.

crystal.reasoning:
I start from the present: Ukraine has just struck the Crimean Bridge in what it calls the biggest drone operation of the war, partially collapsing it and isolating Crimea further. Russia has vowed a 'far more painful response.' Trump met Putin at APEC with Xi hosting, floated Donbas-for-NATO, and wants a deal before January. Zelensky called Putin 'killer' in response to Trump's 'friend.' Europe moved from words to commitments: France sending troops, UK pledging 1,000+ missiles, EU proposing a 45-billion-euro loan. The Starshield dispute is at a personal breaking point between Zelensky and Musk. Russia hit Kyiv and Zelensky's own hometown Kryvyi Rih with a ballistic missile. Winter is closing in and the nuclear safety warning says accident risk is rising.

Now I extend each theme along its motion. The bridge strike was a step-change: Ukraine moved from grinding economic pressure (refineries) to a single symbolic strategic blow. The motion says the next step is for Russia to answer in kind, not just with more of the same barrages but with a visible, painful, possibly new-type response. The diplomatic motion went from envoys to the president himself, and the next step is follow-up: either a second round of talks, a concrete US proposal on security guarantees, or a formal rejection that resets the table. The European motion went from anxiety to commitment; the next step is operationalization: first French soldiers on Ukrainian soil, first UK missiles delivered, the EU loan entering its first procedural steps. The Starshield motion went from technical to personal; the next step is either a forced resolution or a public rupture. The winter-energy motion is monotonic and accelerating: more strikes, more cold, more visible civilian suffering.

I correct for the wind. Last week I underweighted the probability of a single dramatic symbolic event (the bridge) and overweighted slower threads (India, prisoner exchange). I underestimated Europe's willingness to commit concretely. I treated the week as a continuation of the prior trajectory, but the actual week was a step-change. So for next week I should: (1) give a higher probability to another high-profile, symbolic military event on either side, not just 'more of the same'; (2) expect the diplomatic track to produce a concrete, specific move rather than vague 'talks continue'; (3) expect Europe to be more visible and committed than a baseline forecast would suggest; (4) not over-weight the prisoner exchange or slower institutional processes; (5) expect the personal, confrontational tone (Musk-Zelensky, Trump-Putin) to persist rather than cool down; (6) expect the week to be defined by 2-3 dramatic events rather than a steady drift.

The driver for next week is the collision of three deadlines: Russia's promised 'painful response' (immediate, days), the US January deadline for a deal (weeks), and the winter energy crunch (ongoing, worsening). These three compress into the same week. The bridge is now a bargaining chip that Russia must either repair (showing weakness) or answer (showing strength), and the diplomatic table is set but the pieces have not been moved. Europe is no longer waiting at the door; it is walking in with troops and money. The Starshield dispute is a fuse that could either explode into a US political firestorm or be quietly resolved, and either outcome will be newsworthy.

What I would not bet on: a full ceasefire, a Zelensky resignation, a new full-scale Russian ground offensive, a Chernobyl nuclear incident, formal NATO membership, a warship sinking, a snap Ukrainian referendum, or a direct Zelensky-Putin bilateral meeting. These are all still outside the probable range for a single week.
crystal.forecast:
THEMES FOR THE WEEK OF NOVEMBER 21-28, 2026

1. Russia's 'Painful Response' to the Bridge Strikes (Direction: Escalation, Confidence: High)
Russia's Kremlin aide and Putin himself vowed a far more painful response to the Crimean Bridge strikes. The most likely form of that response is another major overnight missile and drone barrage on Ukrainian cities, possibly targeting a new category of infrastructure not yet hit in this intensity: a major railway hub, a military command center, or a second bridge. Given that Zelensky's own hometown Kryvyi Rih was already hit with a ballistic missile, there is a real chance of a strike on a symbolically personal target for Ukraine, perhaps a major industrial city like Kharkiv or Dnipro, or a repeat double-tap on Kyiv. I would not be surprised to see Russia test a new weapon system or a new attack vector (hypersonic glide, a coordinated multi-axis strike) to signal that the response is qualitatively different, not just quantitatively larger. The bridge cleanup will take months, and Russia may use that period to consolidate and reposition in Crimea before the next Ukrainian strike. Confidence: High that there will be at least one major Russian barrage this week. Medium on whether it will be qualitatively new or just larger.

2. Diplomatic Follow-Up to APEC and the Donbas-for-NATO Question (Direction: Active movement toward a concrete proposal, Confidence: Medium-High)
Trump said he wants a peace deal before January. The trilateral at APEC was the first real meeting. The next step is a second round of talks or a concrete US-drafted proposal on security guarantees, the status of Donbas, and the mechanism for enforcement. The Donbas-for-NATO idea is now on the table and Russia has formally rejected NATO membership for Ukraine, but the US may reframe it as 'NATO-style guarantees without a formal Article 5 commitment,' which is what Kushner suggested Russia was comfortable with. I expect at least one visible diplomatic event this week: a second meeting (possibly in a neutral location like Switzerland or the Gulf), a formal US proposal document, or a public exchange between Zelensky and Trump on the territorial question. Europe will push to be included, and Merz's promise to 'join new peace talks soon' suggests a European delegation will be present or in close coordination. The risk is that the talks produce a gap rather than a bridge: Russia wants a security freeze, Ukraine wants a security guarantee, and the US wants to close the file. Confidence: Medium-High for a visible diplomatic event. Medium for a concrete proposal. Low for a signed agreement.

3. European Military Commitments Moving from Pledge to Presence (Direction: Operationalization, Confidence: High)
France is sending soldiers into Ukraine under the Volia mission. The UK has pledged over 1,000 short-range missiles and long-range drones. Germany is backing a new Ukrainian drone production venture. The EU has proposed a 45-billion-euro loan. Eleven European nations held a joint drill in Poland. Next week is the window where at least some of these move from announcement to reality: first French troops arriving in a specific Ukrainian region, first UK missile deliveries rolling off a cargo plane, the EU loan entering its first parliamentary or Council vote. This will generate visible, concrete news: a photo of French soldiers in a Ukrainian uniform, a delivery ceremony, a parliamentary vote. The wind says I should expect Europe to be more committed and visible than a baseline forecast would predict, and the motion confirms that the argument has become action. Confidence: High that at least one European commitment becomes visible and operational this week.

4. Starshield Dispute: Resolution or Rupture (Direction: A decisive development, Confidence: Medium)
The dispute has moved from technical to personal. Zelensky said Musk is restricting Ukraine's ability to counter jet-powered drones. Musk accused Zelensky of lying. Trump's intelligence chief threatened to withhold SpaceX funding. This is a fuse. Next week, one of two things will happen: either the restrictions are lifted (possibly under quiet US pressure) and the dispute fades, or it escalates into a US political firestorm with congressional hearings, a formal US government letter to SpaceX, or Zelensky making a public address directly to the American public. Given the wind, I expect the personal, confrontational tone to persist rather than cool down. A quiet resolution is possible but less likely than a public moment. Confidence: Medium for a notable development. The direction is uncertain (resolution vs. escalation), but the event is likely.

5. Winter Energy Crisis Deepening (Direction: Worsening, Confidence: High)
The nuclear safety warning says the risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine is increasing this winter. Russia is explicitly targeting power plants as winter approaches, the EU says. Kyiv has water and power cuts. The grid is under cumulative stress. Next week, as temperatures drop, the energy crisis will become more visible in daily life: longer blackouts, water rationing, public appeals from mayors, possibly a new round of strikes specifically on substations and thermal plants. The IMF's near-finalised 1.6-billion-dollar deal will be a quiet but important backstop. I expect at least one major energy-related incident and a visible public impact. Confidence: High.

6. Ukrainian Counter-Offensive and New Symbolic Strikes (Direction: Continued offensive, possible new high-profile target, Confidence: Medium)
Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi is described as melding man and machine to repel Russian forces. The bridge strike set a precedent for high-symbol-value targets. Ukraine may look for another: a major port (Odessa or Mariupol), a second bridge, a Russian military airbase in a border region, or a high-value command node. The drone-warfare technology is evolving rapidly (flying modems, drone-ambulances), and Ukraine may deploy a new capability in a visible way. The wind says I should weight a dramatic symbolic event more heavily than a steady grinding advance. Confidence: Medium for another notable Ukrainian strike. Lower for a ground offensive.

7. Intelligence and Information War (Direction: Continued low-level friction, Confidence: Medium)
The Denmark assassination plot, the Palantir spy arrest, and the tear gas investigation are all threads that suggest a growing intelligence-warfront. Next week may bring one more incident: a new espionage arrest, a cyberattack on a European or US target, or the tear gas finding gaining traction as a potential chemical-weapons issue that could trigger a UN or IAEA response. The IAEA controversy over a sanctioned Russian official in a senior nuclear post is a quiet but persistent irritant. Confidence: Medium for at least one intelligence-related news item. Lower for a major escalation.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES THE MOTION MAKES MORE PROBABLE THAN THEY LOOK
- A second Ukrainian strike on another major Russian infrastructure asset (a port, a second bridge, a major railway junction) within the same week, following the bridge precedent. The motion from refineries to bridge suggests the next step is another single high-value target, not a spread of smaller ones.
- A formal US-drafted security-guarantee document, more specific than 'NATO membership,' possibly involving a US or European troop presence on Ukrainian soil in a defined postwar configuration. The Donbas-for-NATO thread needs to be resolved, and the resolution will be a document, not just a statement.
- A visible Russian domestic reaction to the fuel crisis: a fuel queue, a regional governor's public complaint, or a small protest in a city where petrol is rationed. The wind says I should not over-weight this, but the bridge strikes and refinery hits are making the economic squeeze more visible, and a single image of a fuel queue could become a headline.
- Zelensky making a major domestic political move in response to the pressure of the week: a cabinet reshuffle, a public address to the nation, or a specific policy announcement (conscription change, energy rationing, a new defense budget). The personal hit to his hometown and the diplomatic sidelining at APEC create pressure for a visible domestic response.
- A new European country (possibly Spain, Italy, or the Nordics) announcing a specific troop deployment or a new military aid package, following France's Volia mission and the UK's missile pledge.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON
- A full ceasefire or formal peace agreement signed this week.
- Zelensky resigning or being removed.
- A new full-scale Russian ground offensive (a major armored thrust into new territory).
- A Chernobyl or Zaporizhzhia nuclear incident.
- Formal NATO membership for Ukraine.
- A warship sinking in the Black Sea or Baltic.
- A snap Ukrainian referendum on peace terms.
- A direct bilateral Zelensky-Putin meeting (they may be in the same room at a second trilateral, but not alone).
- A major EU sanctions package formally adopted (the 45B loan is not sanctions, and a new sanctions round is a separate process).
crystal.headline: Ukraine Braces for Russia's Promised Painful Response as Europe Sends Troops
emoji_reasons: The diplomatic aftermath of the Trump-Putin-Xi APEC summit and the Donbas-for-NATO question will drive the week's international agenda.
Russia has vowed a far more painful response to the Crimean Bridge strikes, and another major missile and drone barrage on Ukrainian cities is the most likely military event.
France, the UK, Germany, and the EU are moving from pledges to concrete military and financial commitments, with troops and missiles arriving on Ukrainian soil.
crystal.tldr: Expect Russia to deliver a major retaliatory strike on Ukrainian infrastructure this week, and a visible diplomatic follow-up to the APEC summit as the US pushes toward a pre-January deal. European military commitments will move from announcement to reality, with French troops and UK missiles arriving. The Starshield dispute will either resolve or rupture, and the winter energy crisis will deepen.
crystal.eli5:
Ukraine just did something really big: it sent over 1,300 drones at the bridge that connects Russia to Crimea, and part of the bridge fell. Russia said it would hit back hard. So next week, the most likely thing to happen is a big Russian missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities, maybe on a target that hasn't been hit before. Think of it like a game of chess where one player just took a key piece, and the other player is about to make a dramatic move.

At the same time, the US president met the Russian president in China, and they talked about a deal. The idea floating around is that Ukraine gives up some land in the east (the Donbas) and gets a promise that NATO will protect it. Russia doesn't love the NATO part, but the US is trying to get everyone to agree before January. Next week, you'll probably see more meetings, more statements, and maybe a written proposal. Europe is also stepping up: France is sending soldiers, the UK is sending missiles, and the EU is offering a huge loan. These aren't just promises anymore; the stuff is actually moving.

There's also a fight between Ukraine's president and Elon Musk about satellite internet. Ukraine needs it to track fast drones, and Musk's company has been limiting access. They're now publicly calling each other liars. This could either get solved quietly or blow up into a big political argument in the US. And winter is coming, so Russia is hitting power plants and water systems, making daily life harder for ordinary Ukrainians. The cold is the deadline that makes everything else feel urgent.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A hit on a large share of the week's actual events, and its extra specificity often paid off. The Russian kinetic-escalation section was well calibrated: it expected a major overnight barrage, strikes on water infrastructure, a major city reporting power outages, and Zelensky appealing for conservation. The actual week delivered a massive November 20 barrage on Kyiv that damaged two bridges, knocked out water and power, and hit the Dutch and Austrian embassies, followed by a ballistic missile on Kryvyi Rih that killed a seven-year-old and an emergency worker. A's framing of the winter heating crisis and public conservation appeal was directionally right even if the specific 'queues for heating fuel' detail was not a headline. The drone-and-economic section was A's strongest military call: it expected Ukraine to hit at least one more refinery, to expand the target set to a naval or Black Sea/Baltic target, and to strike a major railway junction or pipeline terminal as part of a broader 'logistics chain' campaign. The actual week saw Ukraine hit refineries in Krasnodar and Tatarstan, more Russian regions limit fuel sales, and, most dramatically, partially collapse the Kerch Bridge in a 1,300-drone barrage. A's 'logistics chain' framing is the closest either forecast came to capturing that bridge strike, even though A listed it under 'railway junction or pipeline terminal' rather than naming the bridge. The Starlink section was specific and largely right: A expected a formal hearing, a State Department or Pentagon statement, or a partial restoration with conditions. The actual week brought a public Zelensky-Musk clash, Musk accusing Zelensky of lying, and Trump's intelligence chief warning that no SpaceX funding would flow without answers. A's 'less likely surprise' of a Republican senator or the White House taking a public position was close to the intel-chief intervention. The European institutional section got the five-nation coordination meeting right (the Berlin 'Coalition of the Willing' summit on November 19) and the EU loan right (the 45 billion euro proposal, partly serviced by Russian frozen-asset profits). A's 'less likely surprise' of Zelensky setting a specific referendum date did not quite materialize; he said he was 'ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum' but did not pin down a mid-December date. The US envoy shuttle section was partially right: Witkoff and Kushner were expected in Berlin, and Trump made multiple public statements. But A's framing of 'shuttle diplomacy' as the preferred channel undersold the actual event, which was Trump personally meeting Putin at the APEC summit in a trilateral setting with Xi. A's 'Zelensky-Putin direct phone call is possible but I would not bet on it' was conservative; the trilateral summit was a bigger step than either a phone call or an envoy shuttle. The India-Black Sea thread was A's weakest call: it expected a joint working group, a corridor proposal, or a Modi office statement, none of which appeared as a headline this week. The Russian domestic pressure section expected a security crackdown after the car bombs and a regional governor complaining about economic impact; the car bombs were last week's news and the crackdown was not a headline this week, though Bloomberg's piece on Putin's war ravaging a generation of Russian men fits the broader theme. The Ukrainian domestic politics section expected an opposition rally, regional governors weighing in, and a poll release; these were not the dominant domestic stories, which were instead the referendum debate and the reaction to the Trump-Putin meeting. The economy-and-finance section was directionally right on the EU loan and defense-tech deals (Germany backing Auterion and Skyfall, the UK pledging over 1,000 missiles), though the specific oil-price prediction of a 1-to-3 percent net decline was not a headline. Overall, A's picture was comprehensive and captured most of the week's major threads, with the referendum debate as the anchor. Its main overreach was rating the referendum as 'the single biggest story of the week' when the Crimean Bridge strike and the Trump-Putin-Xi summit were arguably bigger. Its main misses were the India thread, the specific domestic-politics events, and the exact diplomatic format (summit rather than shuttle).
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B was more focused and made fewer, more confident predictions, and most of them came true. The Donbas-for-NATO section was directionally right: B expected Zelensky to consult his cabinet and hint at or schedule a referendum, and he did say he was ready to put the deal to a vote. B expected Putin to use the proposal to pressure Kyiv while downplaying it; the actual week saw Russia rejecting formal NATO membership (Ryabkov) while Kushner said Russia was 'comfortable' with NATO-like guarantees, which is a more nuanced response than B's 'downplaying' framing but in the same spirit. B rated this 'almost certain' as the dominant headline cluster, which is an overstatement given the Bridge and the summit were bigger, but it was certainly a top-three story. The second-round-talks section was B's best diplomatic call: it expected either a second round of trilateral talks or preparatory bilateral meetings. The actual event was the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral at APEC, which is closer to B's 'trilateral talks' framing than to A's 'shuttle diplomacy.' B's 'probable' rating for a second formal round was well calibrated, even if the format (APEC summit hosted by Xi) was beyond what either forecast specified. The prisoner-exchange prediction was B's clearest miss: it expected the first wave of prisoners to be exchanged within the window, with bureaucratic friction and possibly a public ceremony. None of that appeared in the headlines; the exchange was agreed in principle at Abu Dhabi but the logistics did not produce a headline event this week. The Russian strikes section was right and well calibrated at 'almost certain': continued and intensified strikes on energy and water, more blackouts in Kyiv, the 'toughest winter' framing becoming daily reality. The actual barrage on November 20 and the Kryvyi Rih missile hit on November 21 confirmed this. The drone-strikes section was right at 'probable': B expected continued strikes on refineries, pipelines, and storage, with a possible new high-profile strike. The Krasnodar and Tatarstan refinery hits and the spreading fuel rationing confirmed this, though B's framing was narrower than A's 'logistics chain' and did not point toward the Bridge. The Starlink section was right at 'probable': B expected Musk or SpaceX to respond publicly, the US government to intervene, and a possible small political firestorm. The actual Zelensky-Musk clash, the 'lying' accusation, and the Trump intel-chief warning all fit. B's 'probable' rating was well calibrated. The EU budget section was partially right: B expected more public sparring between Germany and eastern EU states and a draft funding package to be tabled. The 45 billion euro loan was tabled, but the Merz-Fico sparring was not the dominant EU story this week; the Berlin summit and the 'Yalta 2.0' optics were bigger. The Baltic-and-maritime section was right at 'possible': B expected at least one more incident in the Baltic or Black Sea. Finland's report of a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian cargo in the Baltic Sea confirmed this. The Russian domestic pressure section was right at 'possible' but not a headline: B expected more visible public frustration, possibly small protests or a more aggressive information campaign. The car-bomb crackdown was not a headline this week, though the broader domestic-cost theme was present. The India section was right at 'possible' but did not materialize as a headline: B expected a concrete proposal or joint statement on Black Sea corridors, which did not appear. B's 'less likely surprises' list was well judged: the Zelensky-Putin meeting (rated 'unlikely but not impossible') was close to the trilateral summit, even if the actual format was bigger. The 'things I would not bet on' list was all correct: no full ceasefire, no Zelensky resignation, no new Russian offensive axis, no Chernobyl incident, no formal NATO membership, no warship sinking in the Baltic. This clean negative list shows good calibration. Overall, B's picture was cleaner and more focused, with better calibration of confidence levels. Its main miss was the prisoner exchange, and its main under-call was the Crimean Bridge (its drone section was narrower than A's). Its main over-call was the prisoner exchange and, to a lesser degree, the India thread. The diplomatic format (trilateral at APEC) was closer to B's framing than to A's.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts captured the broad shape of the week: the Donbas-for-NATO debate, the Russian retaliatory barrage, the Ukrainian drone campaign, the Starlink/Starshield dispute, the European summit, and the EU funding package. Both overrated the referendum as the single dominant story when the Crimean Bridge strike and the Trump-Putin-Xi summit were arguably bigger. Both missed the Bridge as the specific target, though A's 'logistics chain' and 'railway junction or pipeline terminal' framing is closer to the Bridge than B's narrower 'refineries, pipelines, and storage.' Both missed the Denmark assassination plot, Prince Harry's surprise visit, the tear-gas investigation, the IAEA controversy, and the nuclear-safety warning, none of which were dominant stories. On the diplomatic track, B's 'trilateral talks' framing was closer to the actual APEC summit than A's 'shuttle diplomacy,' and B's 'less likely surprise' of a Zelensky-Putin meeting was closer to the trilateral than A's 'phone call possible but I would not bet on it.' On the military track, A was more comprehensive: its drone section covered refineries, naval targets, the Baltic, and logistics infrastructure, which better encompassed the Bridge strike, the Krasnodar and Tatarstan refinery hits, and the Baltic cargo incident. B's drone section was narrower and missed the Bridge and the Baltic. On the Starlink thread, A was more specific (hearing, State Department statement, partial restoration, BT launch, Fire Point funding, Republican senator or White House position) and several of those specifics came true or were close. B was more general but still correct. On the EU/finance thread, A was more specific (joint borrowing mechanism, UForce funding, sovereign bonds) and the 45 billion euro loan and defense-tech deals confirmed those specifics. B was correct but less detailed. On calibration, B had the edge: its 'almost certain,' 'probable,' and 'possible' ratings were well matched to what actually happened, and its 'things I would not bet on' list was entirely correct. A made more predictions, which meant more opportunities to be wrong, and it was wrong on the India thread, the specific domestic-politics events (opposition rally, regional governors, SBU statement), and the car-bomb follow-up. However, A's extra predictions that were right (Starlink specifics, EU loan specifics, logistics framing, Baltic expansion) more than offset the misses. A's overall picture was richer and covered more of the week's actual events, even if it was more scattered. B's picture was cleaner and more focused, with better calibration, but it left out some threads that did materialize (the Baltic, the logistics/bridge angle, the Starlink specifics). For a reader trying to understand the coming week, A's forecast would have provided a more complete map: it pointed toward the Bridge (via logistics), the Baltic, the Starlink political fight, the EU loan, the defense-tech deals, and the European summit. B's forecast would have provided a cleaner, more confident picture of the top five or six stories, with good negative space. The deciding factor is the Crimean Bridge: it was the single biggest military event of the week, and A's framing was closer to it than B's. Combined with A's better coverage of the Starlink specifics, the EU/finance details, and the Baltic, A's picture was more complete. B's better calibration and cleaner structure are real advantages, but they do not fully compensate for the narrower military picture and the prisoner-exchange miss. The difference is small, but A's extra correct detail tips the balance. VERDICT: A
